summary: Describes an architectural framework for network telemetry, which gathers network insight for efficient and automated management. It covers data generation, collection, correlation, and consumption, clarifies terms, and classifies the components of a telemetry system. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Network telemetry is the practice of pulling data out of a network and feeding it to software that acts on it. This RFC sorts that practice into a framework: four modules for where the data comes from, five components that every module has, and four kinds of data. It defines no protocol; its purpose is to give existing and future techniques a common place to fit.

questions: what are the network telemetry modules
subtitle: A shared map of network telemetry: four modules, five components and four kinds of data.

tldr.problem: Networks need to supply much more, and much fresher, data to automated tools than polling-based techniques such as SNMP, the command line and Syslog can provide, and the term network telemetry had no clear definition.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9232 partitions telemetry into four modules by where the data comes from, breaks each into five components with the same structure, and classifies data as simple, derived, event-triggered or streaming.
tldr.outcome: It defines no protocol. It gives a shared taxonomy and a place to map existing mechanisms such as YANG-Push, gNMI, BMP, IPFIX and IOAM onto, so that future work has somewhere to fit.

today: RFC 9232 is an Informational RFC published in May 2022 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines no protocol of its own. Its value is the taxonomy: a place to put existing mechanisms such as YANG-Push, gNMI, BMP, IPFIX and IOAM, and a vocabulary for whatever comes next.

sections.title: What Network Telemetry Means
sections.content:
Network visibility is the ability of management tools to see the state and behaviour of a network, and it is essential to successful network operation. Network telemetry covers network data that can give insight into the current state of the network, including its devices and its forwarding, control and management planes; that can be generated and obtained through a variety of techniques, including network instrumentation and measurement; and that can be processed for purposes ranging from service assurance to network security. In this document the term covers both the data itself, Network Telemetry Data, and the techniques and processes used to generate, export, collect and consume that data for use by potentially automated management applications. It extends beyond the classical Operations, Administration and Management (OAM) techniques and expects to support better flexibility, scalability, accuracy, coverage and performance.

The problem the document sets out to solve is that the term network telemetry lacks an unambiguous definition, and that its scope and coverage cause confusion and misunderstandings. The purpose is to clarify the concept and provide a clear architectural framework, so that the technical field can be articulated and related techniques and standards aligned.

One limit is stated early and applies to everything that follows. Large-scale network data collection is a major threat to user privacy and may be indistinguishable from pervasive monitoring. The framework must not be applied to generating, exporting, collecting, analysing or retaining individual user data, or any data that can identify end users or characterise their behaviour without consent. On that principle the framework is not applicable to networks whose endpoints represent individual users, such as general-purpose access networks. Separately, no user packet content should be collected: the data objects generated, exported and collected should not include any packet payload from traffic associated with end-user systems.

The document also separates two terms that are often used loosely. Network telemetry is considered an extension of OAM rather than a replacement for it: it covers all the existing OAM protocols but puts more emphasis on the newer and emerging techniques and protocols, from data acquisition through to consumption. There is no hard-line distinction between the two concepts.
sections.plainLanguage: The word telemetry comes from the idea of sending readings from a distant place. Here it means network data that is collected from the devices and then handed to software that can act on it, rather than to a person reading a screen. The RFC sets out what the word covers, and where it must not be used: on networks that serve individual people, where collecting this much data would be surveillance.

sections.title: Why the Old Ways Fall Short
sections.content:
The use cases the document names for network operations are security, where intrusion detection and prevention need to watch traffic and activities and act on anomalies; policy and intent compliance, where the rules that constrain services or require flows to pass through an ordered set of network functions have to be verified continuously and any violation reported immediately; SLA compliance, where users need to check they get the service they were promised and operators need real-time telemetry data to evaluate delivery; root cause analysis, where failures are often the effect of a chain of events and the relevant diagnostic data has to be sensed and provided; network optimization, including load balancing, traffic engineering and network planning, where microbursts may need detecting within a very short time frame; and event tracking and prediction, where operators want to learn where and why packets are dropped and to be warned of issues in advance.

For a long time operators have relied on SNMP, the Command-Line Interface or Syslog to monitor the network. The document lists why these are not sufficient. Most use cases need to monitor continuously and refine the data collection in real time, and poll-based low-frequency collection is ill-suited to them; subscription-based streaming pushed from the data source, such as the forwarding chip, is preferred. Comprehensive data is needed, ranging from packet processing engines to traffic managers, line cards to main control boards, user flows to control protocol packets, device configurations to operations and physical layers to application layers, while conventional OAM covers only a narrow range, SNMP handling only Management Information Base data. Many scenarios need to correlate network-wide data from multiple sources, and piecemeal solutions lack the capability to consolidate it. Some conventional techniques lack a formal data model, and unstructured data hinder tool automation. Although some techniques do support data push, such as SNMP Trap, Syslog and sFlow, the pushed data are limited to predefined management plane warnings or sampled user packets, while operators need data with arbitrary source, granularity and precision. Passive measurement can consume excessive resources and produce redundant data or give inaccurate results, while active measurement can interfere with user traffic and gives only indirect results.

The document then lists the characteristics that have been accepted for network telemetry. It is push and streaming: collectors subscribe to data pushed from data sources instead of polling. It has volume and velocity: the data is consumed by machines rather than by people, so the volume can be huge and processing is optimised for automation in real time. It aims at normalization and unification, so that analysis can work across heterogeneous devices and data sources. It is model-based, with data modelled in advance so applications can configure and consume it easily. It supports data fusion, where the data for one application comes from several sources, across domains, devices and layers, that share a common name or identifier and have to be correlated. And it is dynamic and interactive, running continuously and adapting to queries from the network operation controller.
sections.plainLanguage: Polling a device every few seconds is too slow and too narrow for software that has to spot a problem and act on it. The document lists what automated operations need: continuous streams, data from every part of the device, a defined structure so tools can read it, and a way to join data from different places into one picture.

sections.title: Four Modules
sections.content:
The framework partitions network telemetry into four modules based on the source of the telemetry data object, and gives each its own interface to network operation applications. The modules are Management Plane Telemetry, Control Plane Telemetry, Forwarding Plane Telemetry and External Data and Event Telemetry. The partition rests on the different data objects involved, which lead to different data sources and export locations. Those differences have deep implications for in-network data programming and processing, for data encoding and the transport protocol, and for the data bandwidth and latency required. Data can be sent directly or proxied through the control and management planes, and each approach has advantages and disadvantages.

The document compares the modules along six angles: data object, data export location, data model, data encoding, telemetry application protocol and data transport method. Management plane telemetry covers configuration and operation state, and is exported from the main control CPU with data models such as YANG, MIB and Syslog, encoded with GPB, JSON or XML, and carried by gRPC, NETCONF or RESTCONF over HTTP(S) or TCP. Control plane telemetry covers control protocol and signalling state and the routing information base, exported from the main control CPU, the linecard CPU or the forwarding chip, with YANG or custom models, and carried by gRPC, NETCONF or IPFIX, or by traffic mirroring, over HTTP(S), TCP or UDP. Forwarding plane telemetry covers flow and packet data, quality of service, traffic statistics, buffer and queue statistics, the forwarding information base and access control lists; it is exported from the forwarding chip, the linecard CPU or the main control CPU, and the table gives plain text encoding, IPFIX, traffic mirroring, gRPC or NetFlow, over UDP. External data telemetry covers terminal, social and environmental data, exported from various places, with YANG or custom models, GPB, JSON, XML or plain text encoding, gRPC as the application protocol and HTTP(S), TCP or UDP as transport.

The reasoning behind the differences is practical. The forwarding chip has high throughput but limited capacity for complex data and state, while the main control CPU can do complex data and state processing but has limited bandwidth for high throughput data, so the suitable telemetry protocol differs per module. The document's conclusion is that one cannot expect a universal protocol to cover all network telemetry requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Data comes from four places: what the device is configured to do, what its routing protocols are doing, what its forwarding hardware is doing, and what happens outside the network entirely. Each place has its own data, its own natural export point and its own limits, so the framework keeps them as separate modules instead of forcing one mechanism on all of them.

sections.title: Five Components in Every Module
sections.content:
Each module is further partitioned into five conceptual components, and the same structure applies in every one of them.

  • Data Query, Analysis, and Storage. This component works at the network operation application block. It is normally part of the network management system on the receiver side. It issues data requirements, which can be modelled data through configuration or custom data through programming, and the requirements are either queries for one-shot data or subscriptions for events or streaming data. It also receives, stores and processes the returned data. Analysis can be interactive and start further queries. The component can live in network devices or in remote controllers, and can be centralised or distributed with one or more instances.
  • Data Configuration and Subscription. This manages the data queries on devices. It determines the protocol and the channel for applications to acquire the data they want, and it configures the data that might not be directly available from the data sources. A subscription can be described by models, templates or programs.
  • Data Encoding and Export. This determines how the data is delivered to the analysis and storage component, with access control. The encoding and the transport protocol may vary with the export location.
  • Data Generation and Processing. The requested data has to be captured, filtered, processed and formatted inside the device from the raw sources. This may involve in-network computing on either the fast path or the slow path.
  • Data Object and Source. This determines the monitoring objects and the original data sources provisioned in the device. A data source usually provides raw data that needs further processing, and each can be considered a probe. Some can be installed dynamically, others are more static.

The framework also maps existing work onto itself. In the management plane, gNMI, NETCONF, RESTCONF, SNMP and YANG-Push handle data configuration and subscription, MIB and YANG handle data generation, and gRPC, HTTP and TCP handle encoding and export. The control plane has the same configuration set, YANG for generation, and BMP over TCP for encoding and export. The forwarding plane uses NETCONF, RESTCONF and YANG-Push for configuration, IOAM, PSAMP, PBT and Alternate Marking for generation, and IPFIX over UDP for encoding and export. The document notes that the list is not exhaustive and that a name in a block emphasises only one characteristic of a protocol that may cover more.
sections.plainLanguage: Every module has the same five moving parts: something asks for data, something decides what will be sent and how it is subscribed to, something encodes and ships it, something inside the device gathers and formats it, and something identifies the raw source it came from. Existing protocols slot into these five parts, and the table in the RFC shows where each one lands.

sections.title: Push or Pull, and Four Kinds of Data
sections.content:
Network data can be acquired through subscription, which is push, and through query, which is poll. A subscription is a contract between publisher and subscriber: after the initial setup the subscribed data is delivered automatically to registered subscribers until the subscription expires. Subscriptions can be predefined, or the subscriber can configure and tailor the published data to its needs. Queries are used when a client expects immediate, one-off feedback; the queried data may be extracted directly from a data source or synthesised from raw data, and they work well for interactive applications. In general data can be pulled whenever needed, but pushing is often more efficient and reduces the latency of a client detecting a change.

From the consumer's point of view there are four types of data. Simple Data is steadily available from a datastore or from static probes. Derived Data has to be synthesised or processed in the network from raw data from one or more devices, with the processing function loaded statically or dynamically. Event-triggered Data is acquired conditionally on the occurrence of an event, such as an interface changing operational state between up and down, and can be pushed by subscription or polled by query; there are many ways to model events, including with a Finite State Machine or Event-Condition-Action policy. Streaming Data is generated continuously, as a time series or a dump of databases, for example an interface packet counter exported every second; it reflects real-time network states and metrics, needs large bandwidth and processing power, and is always actively pushed.

These types are not mutually exclusive but are often composite: derived data is composed of simple data, event-triggered data can be simple or derived, and streaming data can be based on some recurring event. Subscription usually deals with event-triggered and streaming data, and query usually deals with simple and derived data, although the other combinations are possible. Advanced telemetry techniques are designed mainly for event-triggered or streaming data subscription and for derived data query.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to get data. A subscription means the device sends it as it changes; a query means the client asks once and waits for an answer. The four kinds of data differ in where they come from: already sitting in a table, calculated on the way out, produced when something happens, or produced continuously.

sections.title: How Telemetry Evolves, and Its Risks
sections.content:
The document describes four stages in the evolution of network telemetry applications as the network moves towards automated operation. Each stage builds on the techniques of the previous one plus new requirements. Stage 0, Static Telemetry: the telemetry data source and type are determined at design time, and the operator can only configure how it is used, with limited flexibility. Stage 1, Dynamic Telemetry: custom telemetry data can be dynamically programmed or configured at runtime without interrupting network operation, allowing a trade-off among resource, performance, flexibility and coverage. Stage 2, Interactive Telemetry: the operator can continuously customise and fine-tune the telemetry data in real time to reflect visibility requirements; compared with Stage 1 the changes are frequent, based on real-time feedback, and some tasks can be automated, but human operators still sit in the middle to make decisions. Stage 3, Closed-Loop Telemetry: the telemetry is free from the interference of human operators except for generating the reports; the operation engine issues the telemetry data requests, analyses the data and updates the network operations in closed control loops. Existing technologies are ready for Stages 0 and 1, and individual applications for Stages 2 and 3 are possible now, but future autonomic networks may need a comprehensive operation management system working at those stages. A well-defined framework is the first step in that direction.

The security considerations are significant because the framework's mechanisms are more extensive than conventional OAM in both message frequency and traffic amount. Telemetry data can be manipulated to exhaust network resources at each plane and at the data consumer; falsified or tampered data can mislead the decision-making process and paralyse networks; and wrong configuration and programming for telemetry is equally harmful. The telemetry data is highly sensitive and exposes a lot about the network and its configuration, and some of that information can make designing attacks much easier, for instance exact details of what software and patches are installed, and can tell an attacker whether a device may be subject to unprotected vulnerabilities.

The specific protocols, data formats and configurations chosen to implement the framework will dictate the specific security considerations. The document lists the areas they may include: trust and policy models for the framework; role management and access control for enabling and disabling telemetry capabilities; the protocol transport used for telemetry data and its inherent security capabilities; telemetry data stores, storage encryption, methods of access and retention practices; tracking telemetry events and abnormalities that might identify malicious attacks; authentication and integrity protection of telemetry data; and segregating telemetry traffic from the data traffic carried over the network, as management access and management data were historically carried over an independent management network. Some of these may be minimised or negated by policy management. Separating telemetry capabilities into different classes of policy, such as Role-Based Access Control and Event-Condition-Action policies, would help, and potential conflicts between telemetry mechanisms must be detected accurately and resolved quickly so that unnecessary telemetry traffic does not escalate into a denial-of-service attack. Further study is required, and the expectation is that security mechanisms and protocols are developed and deployed along with a telemetry system.
sections.plainLanguage: The document imagines telemetry getting more automatic in four steps: fixed at design time, then programmable while running, then adjusted in real time by people, and finally run as a closed loop by the network itself with no human in the loop. It also warns that telemetry data is sensitive and can be tampered with, and that it can be used to overload the network it is measuring.

viz.caption: THE FIVE COMPONENTS EVERY MODULE HAS

layers.label: Data Query, Analysis and Storage
layers.detail: Issues the data requirements, then receives, stores and processes what comes back.

layers.label: Data Configuration and Subscription
layers.detail: Decides the protocol, the channel and the subscription for each data set.

layers.label: Data Encoding and Export
layers.detail: Delivers the telemetry data to the collector, with access control.

layers.label: Data Generation and Processing
layers.detail: Captures, filters, processes and formats the raw data inside the device.

layers.label: Data Object and Source
layers.detail: The monitoring objects and the raw data sources, each of which acts as a probe.

viz.caption: THE FOUR KINDS OF TELEMETRY DATA

items.label: Steadily available
items.desc: Data that is already there, from a datastore or a static probe.

items.label: Computed in the network
items.desc: Data synthesised or processed in the network from raw data, with the function loaded statically or dynamically.

items.label: Produced by an event
items.desc: Data acquired when something happens, such as an interface changing state between up and down.

items.label: Continuous
items.desc: Data generated continuously, such as a packet counter exported every second; always pushed to subscribers.
